questions.question: According to the lecture, how do primitives compare in shallow equality?
options: By value
By memory address
By type only
By reference
questions.explanation: Primitives compare by value in shallow equality as stated in the lecture.

questions.question: How do objects, arrays, and functions compare in shallow equality?
options: By type
By reference
By content
By value
questions.explanation: Objects, arrays, and functions compare by reference in shallow equality.

questions.question: If a parent component creates a new object literal on every render and passes it as a prop, what will React.memo do?
options: Throw an error
Skip the child re-render
Memoize the object automatically
Re-render the child component
questions.explanation: React.memo re-renders because the new object literal has a new reference failing shallow equality.

questions.question: Why does React.memo re-render a child if a new function is passed as a prop every time?
options: Because functions are always memoized
Because functions compare by value and the value changes
Because React.memo ignores functions
Because functions compare by reference and the reference changes
questions.explanation: Functions compare by reference, so a new function instance causes React.memo to re-render.

questions.question: What is a pitfall of relying on shallow equality when passing props to React.memo components?
options: Primitives are compared by reference causing bugs
New object or function references cause unnecessary re-renders
React.memo cannot memoize primitive props
React.memo does deep equality checks causing slowdowns
questions.explanation: New references for objects or functions cause React.memo to re-render despite unchanged data.

questions.question: Why might React.memo fail to optimize a child component even if props appear unchanged?
options: Because shallow equality fails when new references are passed for objects or functions
Because React.memo requires deep equality checking
Because React.memo ignores props on every render
Because React.memo only works for primitive props
questions.explanation: React.memo relies on shallow equality and fails if new references are passed as props.

questions.question: What does React.memo do by default when a component's props have not changed?
options: Throws an error
Always re-renders the component
Removes the component from the DOM
Skips the component's re-render
questions.explanation: React.memo skips re-rendering when props are shallowly equal to the previous render.

questions.question: When does React.memo cause a component to re-render?
options: Only on initial mount
When props are not shallowly equal to previous props
Never re-renders after first render
When the component state changes
questions.explanation: React.memo re-renders if props differ by shallow equality from the previous render.

questions.question: If a child component wrapped in React.memo receives a new function prop on every parent render, what happens?
options: The child re-renders because the function reference changes
The child skips re-render because functions are ignored
The child memoizes the function automatically
The child throws an error
questions.explanation: New function references cause React.memo to re-render the child component.

questions.question: How can you prevent a React.memo child from re-rendering due to a changing callback prop?
options: Use useMemo instead of useCallback
Pass a new function on every render
Avoid passing callbacks as props
Wrap the callback in useCallback to keep its reference stable
questions.explanation: useCallback keeps the function reference stable, preventing unnecessary re-renders.

questions.question: What is a trade-off of wrapping every child component in React.memo?
options: It adds overhead and dependency bugs without benefit if the child is cheap to render
It guarantees no re-renders ever occur
It removes the need for useCallback or useMemo
It automatically memoizes all props deeply
questions.explanation: Memoizing every component can add overhead and bugs if the child is not expensive to render.

questions.question: Why is React.memo ineffective if the parent passes new object or function literals every render?
options: Because React.memo does deep equality checks
Because React.memo only works with primitive props
Because React.memo ignores props
Because shallow equality fails and React.memo re-renders the child
questions.explanation: New references cause shallow equality to fail, defeating React.memo optimization.

questions.question: What does useCallback do in React?
options: Forces a component to re-render
Keeps a function reference stable across renders if dependencies don't change
Creates a new function on every render
Memoizes a computed value
questions.explanation: useCallback memoizes a function reference and returns the same function unless dependencies change.

questions.question: When should you use useCallback according to the lecture?
options: When you want to recompute a value every render
When you want to create a new function every render
When passing callbacks to memoized child components
When memoizing computed values
questions.explanation: useCallback is needed to keep callbacks stable when passed to React.memo children.

questions.question: If a parent component passes a callback prop wrapped in useCallback to a React.memo child, what is the effect?
options: The child always re-renders
The callback is recomputed every render
The child sees a stable prop and can skip re-rendering
The child throws an error
questions.explanation: useCallback keeps the function reference stable, enabling React.memo to skip re-render.

questions.question: What happens if you don't use useCallback when passing a callback to a React.memo child?
options: The child re-renders because it receives a new function reference every render
The child never re-renders
The callback is ignored
The child memoizes the callback automatically
questions.explanation: Without useCallback, a new function reference causes React.memo to re-render the child.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of overusing useCallback everywhere?
options: It adds overhead and dependency bugs for no benefit
It memoizes computed values instead of functions
It prevents all re-renders
It guarantees better performance always
questions.explanation: Overusing useCallback adds overhead and can cause bugs without improving performance.

questions.question: Why is useCallback necessary in combination with React.memo?
options: To create new functions every render
To force component re-renders
To keep function references stable so React.memo can skip re-renders
To memoize computed values
questions.explanation: useCallback keeps the function reference stable, which is required for React.memo optimizations.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of useMemo in React?
options: Memoizing a computed value and recomputing only when dependencies change
Always recomputing a value every render
Forcing a component to re-render
Memoizing a function reference
questions.explanation: useMemo memoizes computed values and only recomputes them when dependencies change.

questions.question: When is useMemo particularly valuable?
options: For memoizing callbacks passed to children
For forcing updates on every render
For expensive computed state derived from props or state that would otherwise recalculate every render
For creating new objects every render
questions.explanation: useMemo avoids recomputing expensive derived state when inputs have not changed.

questions.question: If you have a filtered and sorted list derived from a large array, how does useMemo help?
options: It memoizes the filter and sort functions
It skips recomputing the filter and sort if dependencies haven't changed
It recomputes filter and sort on every render
It prevents the component from rendering
questions.explanation: useMemo prevents redundant filter and sort computations if dependencies are unchanged.

questions.question: What happens if you do not use useMemo for expensive computations in React?
options: The computation is memoized by default
The computation is skipped automatically
The component never re-renders
The computation runs on every render even if inputs haven't changed
questions.explanation: Without useMemo, expensive computations run on every render regardless of input changes.

questions.question: What is a main pitfall of overusing useMemo everywhere without profiling?
options: It prevents all re-renders
It guarantees better performance in all cases
It memoizes function references instead of values
It adds overhead from dependency comparisons that can be slower than recomputing
questions.explanation: Overusing useMemo adds overhead that can degrade performance if not needed.

questions.question: Why might useMemo not improve performance if used excessively?
options: Because the cost of dependency comparison can outweigh recomputation savings
Because useMemo disables React.memo
Because useMemo memoizes functions instead of values
Because useMemo always recomputes values
questions.explanation: Dependency comparisons add overhead that can make useMemo slower than recomputing.

questions.question: What happens when you access a property that does not exist directly on a JavaScript object?
options: JavaScript throws an error immediately.
JavaScript copies the property from another object.
JavaScript creates the property on the object automatically.
JavaScript looks up the property on the object's prototype chain until found or null is reached.
questions.explanation: JavaScript walks up the prototype chain automatically until it finds the property or reaches null.

questions.question: What is the internal link every JavaScript object has to another object called?
options: __proto__
hidden class
constructor
prototype
questions.explanation: Every JavaScript object has an internal link called __proto__ pointing to its prototype.

questions.question: If object A has object B as its prototype, and you call a method on A that does not exist on A, what happens?
options: JavaScript copies the method from B to A.
JavaScript stops searching and returns undefined immediately.
JavaScript delegates the lookup to B's properties and methods at runtime.
JavaScript throws a reference error.
questions.explanation: The prototype chain acts as a delegation chain, so lookup is delegated to B at runtime.

questions.question: How does prototype inheritance help with memory efficiency in JavaScript?
options: Prototype chains are copied into each object at creation.
Each object stores its own copy of all methods.
All instances share one copy of inherited methods instead of each having their own copy.
Properties are copied to each instance only when accessed.
questions.explanation: Prototype inheritance delegates lookups so methods are shared, saving memory.

questions.question: What is the role of the 'instanceof' operator in relation to prototype chains?
options: It creates a new instance of a class.
It checks if an object was derived from a particular constructor by walking the prototype chain.
It modifies the prototype chain of an object.
It copies prototype properties to the object.
questions.explanation: 'instanceof' relies on the prototype chain to verify inheritance from a constructor.

questions.question: What issue might arise if you accidentally shadow a prototype method on an object?
options: JavaScript will throw an error when accessing the method.
The object's own property will hide the prototype method, leading to unexpected behavior.
The prototype chain will be broken.
The prototype method will override the object's property.
questions.explanation: Shadowing means the object's own property hides the prototype method during lookup.

questions.question: What does the 'class' keyword in JavaScript do under the hood?
options: It creates a new inheritance mechanism unrelated to prototypes.
It disables prototype inheritance.
It copies methods to each instance explicitly.
It sets up prototype chains and is syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance.
questions.explanation: The class keyword is syntactic sugar that sets up prototype chains behind the scenes.

questions.question: When you write 'class Dog extends Animal', what prototype relationship is established?
options: Dog.prototype has Animal.prototype as its prototype.
Animal.prototype has Dog.prototype as its prototype.
Dog and Animal prototypes are unrelated.
Dog.prototype copies Animal.prototype methods.
questions.explanation: Dog.prototype's prototype is set to Animal.prototype to establish inheritance.

questions.question: How would you explain the relationship between class syntax and prototype inheritance to a beginner?
options: Class syntax is unrelated to prototypes and uses a different mechanism.
Class syntax creates copies of methods for each object instead of using prototypes.
Class syntax disables prototype inheritance.
Class syntax is just a nicer way to write code that uses prototype chains underneath.
questions.explanation: Class syntax is syntactic sugar over prototype chains, making code easier to write and read.

questions.question: If you override a method in a subclass declared with class syntax, how does JavaScript find the method when called on an instance?
options: It first looks on the instance's own properties, then on the subclass prototype, then up the prototype chain.
It copies the superclass method to the instance.
It always calls the method on the superclass prototype.
It throws an error if the method is overridden.
questions.explanation: JavaScript walks the prototype chain from instance to subclass prototype to superclass prototype.

questions.question: Why is the class keyword considered only syntactic sugar and not a new inheritance model?
options: Because it uses a hidden class instead of prototypes.
Because it sets up the same prototype chain mechanism as traditional constructor functions.
Because it disables prototype inheritance.
Because it copies properties instead of delegating.
questions.explanation: Class syntax uses the same prototype chain mechanism, just with nicer syntax.

questions.question: What would happen if Dog.prototype did not have Animal.prototype as its prototype in class inheritance?
options: Instances of Dog would not inherit methods from Animal, breaking expected inheritance.
Dog.prototype would copy Animal.prototype methods instead.
Dog would still inherit Animal's methods correctly.
JavaScript would throw an error at runtime.
questions.explanation: Without linking Dog.prototype to Animal.prototype, inheritance from Animal is broken.

questions.question: What does V8 create internally to describe the shape of an object?
options: A prototype chain
A call stack
A hidden class
A dictionary mode
questions.explanation: V8 creates hidden classes internally to represent object shapes for optimization.

questions.question: When you add a new property to an object in V8, what happens to the hidden class?
options: The object switches to dictionary mode immediately.
The property is added without changing the hidden class.
The hidden class remains unchanged.
V8 creates a new hidden class and transitions the object to it.
questions.explanation: Adding a property causes V8 to create a new hidden class and transition the object.

questions.question: If object A adds properties x then y, and object B adds y then x, what does V8 do?
options: Copies properties from one object to another.
Throws an error for inconsistent property order.
Assigns different hidden classes to A and B due to different property addition order.
Assigns the same hidden class to both objects.
questions.explanation: Different property addition order causes different hidden classes in V8.

questions.question: Why is it bad to add properties dynamically after object construction in V8?
options: Because it deletes existing properties.
Because it causes hidden class transitions that hurt performance in hot code paths.
Because it breaks the prototype chain.
Because it throws runtime errors.
questions.explanation: Dynamic property addition triggers hidden class transitions, slowing performance.

questions.question: What is the recommended practice to optimize object property access in V8?
options: Avoid setting properties to null.
Use the delete operator frequently.
Add properties dynamically in conditionals.
Initialize all object properties in the constructor in the same order every time.
questions.explanation: Consistent property initialization order allows V8 to share hidden classes and optimize access.

questions.question: Why should you avoid using the delete operator on object properties in V8?
options: Because it causes syntax errors.
Because it forces V8 to switch to slower dictionary mode.
Because it breaks the prototype chain.
Because it deletes the hidden class.
questions.explanation: Deleting properties forces V8 to use dictionary mode, reducing performance.

questions.question: What components make up the event loop in JavaScript?
options: Multiple call stacks and a microtask queue.
A single call stack and a macrotask queue.
A hidden class and a prototype chain.
A call stack and multiple threads.
questions.explanation: The event loop consists of a single call stack plus a macrotask queue.

questions.question: When does the event loop take the next macrotask from the queue?
options: When the call stack is empty.
While the call stack is busy.
Immediately after the current function call.
After the microtask queue is empty but before the call stack empties.
questions.explanation: The event loop runs the next macrotask only after the call stack empties.

questions.question: If a long synchronous task runs on the call stack, what is the effect on the page?
options: The microtask queue runs before the long task.
The page updates continuously.
The event loop runs other tasks in parallel.
The page freezes because the event loop cannot process other tasks.
questions.explanation: Long synchronous work blocks the call stack, freezing the page.

questions.question: How does the event loop handle tasks from the macrotask queue?
options: It runs each macrotask to completion before moving to the next.
It interrupts macrotasks to run microtasks.
It runs multiple macrotasks concurrently.
It runs macrotasks only after microtasks are empty.
questions.explanation: Each macrotask is run to completion before the event loop processes the next one.

questions.question: What is the consequence of scheduling many microtasks that schedule more microtasks?
options: The call stack empties faster.
The event loop switches to multiple threads.
The macrotask queue runs first.
The microtask queue can starve the macrotask queue and block rendering.
questions.explanation: Microtasks have higher priority and can starve macrotasks if scheduled continuously.

questions.question: Why is it important that tasks run to completion in the event loop?
options: Because tasks run in parallel threads.
Because tasks are copied before running.
Because tasks are never interrupted, preventing inconsistent state.
Because tasks can be paused and resumed arbitrarily.
questions.explanation: Tasks run to completion to avoid interruption and maintain consistent state.

questions.question: Which queue do promises use to schedule their callbacks?
options: The hidden class queue
The macrotask queue
The microtask queue
The call stack
questions.explanation: Promises schedule callbacks in the microtask queue, which has higher priority.

questions.question: When does the microtask queue run in relation to the macrotask queue?
options: Only when the call stack is empty.
Before every macrotask starts.
Only after all macrotasks complete.
After every macrotask finishes and before the next macrotask runs.
questions.explanation: The microtask queue fully drains after each macrotask and before the next macrotask.

questions.question: Why does a resolved Promise's .then callback run before a setTimeout callback scheduled at the same time?
options: Because promises use the macrotask queue.
Because setTimeout is synchronous.
Because setTimeout callbacks run immediately.
Because microtasks have higher priority and run before macrotasks.
questions.explanation: Microtasks (Promise callbacks) run before macrotasks (setTimeout callbacks).

questions.question: What happens if microtasks schedule more microtasks continuously?
options: The microtasks are discarded.
The event loop switches to macrotasks immediately.
The microtask queue can starve the macrotask queue, blocking rendering.
The call stack empties faster.
questions.explanation: Continuous microtask scheduling can starve macrotasks, blocking rendering.

questions.question: How does 'await' relate to microtasks in JavaScript?
options: 'await' blocks the call stack synchronously.
'await' runs code in the macrotask queue.
'await' is syntax sugar over .then, so code after await runs as a microtask.
'await' disables the microtask queue.
questions.explanation: 'await' uses Promise.then internally, scheduling continuation as a microtask.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of microtask starvation in the event loop?
options: Rendering and macrotasks get blocked, causing UI freezes.
Microtasks run slower than macrotasks.
Microtasks are ignored by the event loop.
The call stack overflows immediately.
questions.explanation: Starving macrotasks with microtasks blocks rendering and UI updates.

questions.question: What type of HTTP request initiates a WebSocket connection?
options: PUT
POST
GET
DELETE
questions.explanation: A WebSocket connection begins with a regular HTTP GET request including the Upgrade: websocket header.

questions.question: Which header must be included in the initial HTTP request to ask the server to switch to a WebSocket connection?
options: Accept-Encoding: gzip
Content-Type: application/json
Connection: close
Upgrade: websocket
questions.explanation: The client includes the Upgrade: websocket header to request the server to upgrade the HTTP connection to a WebSocket.

questions.question: If a browser sends a GET request with Upgrade: websocket but omits the Sec-WebSocket-Key header, what is likely to happen?
options: The server rejects the upgrade request
The server responds with 404 Not Found
The server switches to HTTP/2
The server upgrades the connection anyway
questions.explanation: The Sec-WebSocket-Key header is required for the server to validate and accept the upgrade; omitting it causes the server to reject the upgrade.

questions.question: In a scenario where a WebSocket URL starts with ws://, what protocol does the initial handshake use?
options: FTP
HTTPS
HTTP
SMTP
questions.explanation: The initial handshake for a WebSocket connection uses HTTP even if the URL starts with ws://.

questions.question: Why does the WebSocket handshake start as a regular HTTP GET request before upgrading?
options: Because WebSocket URLs are not supported by browsers
To encrypt the connection from the start
To allow proxies to cache the connection
To reuse existing HTTP infrastructure for initial connection
questions.explanation: The handshake starts as a regular HTTP GET to reuse existing HTTP infrastructure and then upgrades to WebSocket.

questions.question: What could be a pitfall if a proxy server does not support the Upgrade: websocket header in the initial HTTP request?
options: The server will ignore the header and accept the connection
The WebSocket connection will silently downgrade to HTTP/2
The client will retry with a POST request
The handshake will fail and the connection won't upgrade
questions.explanation: If a proxy does not support Upgrade: websocket, the handshake fails and the connection cannot upgrade to WebSocket.

questions.question: What HTTP status code does the server send to confirm it is switching protocols to WebSocket?
options: 500 Internal Server Error
404 Not Found
101 Switching Protocols
200 OK
questions.explanation: The server responds with 101 Switching Protocols to confirm the upgrade to WebSocket.

questions.question: What header does the server send in response to the Sec-WebSocket-Key to confirm the handshake?
options: Upgrade
Connection
Sec-WebSocket-Key
Sec-WebSocket-Accept
questions.explanation: The server sends Sec-WebSocket-Accept derived from the client's key to confirm the handshake.

questions.question: If a client receives a Sec-WebSocket-Accept header that does not match the expected value, what should it do?
options: Reject the connection as invalid
Proceed with the connection
Retry the handshake
Ignore the header and send data
questions.explanation: The client verifies the Sec-WebSocket-Accept to ensure it's talking to a genuine server and rejects invalid responses.

questions.question: After the handshake completes, what kind of communication does the WebSocket connection support?
options: Client-to-server requests only
Full-duplex communication in both directions
Server-to-client responses only
Unidirectional broadcast from server
questions.explanation: Once the handshake completes, the connection is full-duplex allowing both sides to send frames anytime.

questions.question: Why does the server concatenate a fixed GUID string to the Sec-WebSocket-Key before hashing it?
options: To convert the key to lowercase
To create a unique accept token for validation
To compress the key for faster transmission
To encrypt the key for security
questions.explanation: The server concatenates a fixed GUID to the key and hashes it to create a unique Sec-WebSocket-Accept for validation.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall if a client does not verify the Sec-WebSocket-Accept header properly?
options: The connection might be vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks
The handshake will automatically retry
The client will send duplicate frames
The server will close the connection immediately
questions.explanation: Not verifying Sec-WebSocket-Accept can cause the client to connect to a misconfigured proxy or attacker, risking security.

questions.question: In long-polling, what does the server do with the client's HTTP request?
options: Sends a 404 error
Responds immediately with cached data
Holds the request open until data is available
Closes the connection immediately
questions.explanation: The server deliberately holds the client's request open until new data is available in long-polling.

questions.question: What happens immediately after the server responds to a long-polling request with data?
options: The client closes the connection
The server upgrades the connection to WebSocket
The client stops requesting data
The client sends another request to wait for more data
questions.explanation: After receiving data, the client instantly sends another request to simulate a continuous connection.

questions.question: If a client wants to simulate a push notification using HTTP but cannot use WebSockets, which method should it use?
options: HTTP/2 Server Push
Long-polling
FTP
Polling
questions.explanation: Long-polling simulates push by holding requests open and immediately re-requesting after a response.

questions.question: How does long-polling affect server resource usage compared to WebSockets in a high-frequency update scenario?
options: It uses the same resources as WebSockets
It reduces CPU usage by caching responses
It uses fewer resources because connections close quickly
It uses more resources due to repeated HTTP requests
questions.explanation: Long-polling uses more resources because each message requires a full HTTP request and response cycle.

questions.question: What is a drawback of long-polling related to the timing of messages?
options: The server can push data without client requests
There is a gap between responses during client reconnects
Messages are sent in both directions simultaneously
Messages are delivered instantly without delay
questions.explanation: Long-polling has a gap between responses where the client reconnects, causing latency.

questions.question: Why might long-polling fail or perform poorly behind some proxies?
options: Proxies upgrade the connection to WebSocket automatically
Proxies cache all long-polling responses
Proxies block all HTTP GET requests
Proxies may close idle connections before data arrives
questions.explanation: Some proxies close idle connections held open by long-polling, disrupting the simulated push mechanism.

questions.question: Which method uses a single long-lived full-duplex connection with minimal framing overhead?
options: Long-polling
WebSocket
HTTP/1.1 keep-alive
Polling
questions.explanation: WebSocket uses one long-lived full-duplex connection with tiny framing overhead after the handshake.

questions.question: What is a characteristic of long-polling compared to WebSockets in terms of HTTP requests?
options: Long-polling sends no HTTP requests
Long-polling uses UDP packets instead of HTTP
Long-polling uses a single HTTP request for all messages
Long-polling sends one HTTP request per message
questions.explanation: Long-polling sends a full HTTP request for each message, unlike WebSocket's persistent connection.

questions.question: In a chat application with frequent bidirectional messages, which method is more efficient and why?
options: WebSocket, because it uses multiple TCP connections
Long-polling, because it works through old proxies
Long-polling, because it uses simple HTTP requests
WebSocket, because it maintains a single full-duplex connection with low overhead
questions.explanation: WebSocket is more efficient for frequent bidirectional traffic due to its single persistent connection and low framing overhead.

questions.question: Why might long-polling still be used despite WebSockets' efficiency advantages?
options: It uses less bandwidth for high-frequency updates
It has lower latency than WebSockets
It is simpler and works through old proxies
It supports full-duplex communication
questions.explanation: Long-polling is simpler and compatible with old proxies, making it suitable for some use cases.

questions.question: What is a trade-off when choosing long-polling over WebSockets for real-time updates?
options: Long-polling encrypts data by default while WebSockets do not
Long-polling requires multiple HTTP requests causing overhead and reconnect gaps
Long-polling has lower overhead but higher latency
Long-polling supports full-duplex communication unlike WebSockets
questions.explanation: Long-polling pays the overhead of repeated HTTP requests and has gaps during reconnects, unlike WebSockets.

questions.question: What might happen if a WebSocket connection drops and the client falls back to long-polling?
options: The client will gain full-duplex communication
The client will experience increased latency and overhead due to reconnects
The client will stop receiving updates
The server will close all connections immediately
questions.explanation: Falling back to long-polling increases overhead and latency because of repeated HTTP requests and reconnect gaps.

questions.question: What does running npm link inside a library directory do?
options: It publishes the package to the npm registry.
It registers the package globally by creating a global symlink.
It installs the package locally in the consuming project.
It deletes the package from the global node_modules.
questions.explanation: Running npm link inside a library registers it by creating a global symlink from the package into the global node_modules.

questions.question: Where is the global symlink created by npm link stored?
options: In the global node_modules directory.
In the library's source folder.
In the npm registry.
In the local project node_modules directory.
questions.explanation: npm link creates a global symlink from your library package to your global node_modules.

questions.question: If you run npm link inside your library but forget to run npm link <package-name> in your consuming project, what happens?
options: The consuming project will use the latest published version from npm.
The library will be published automatically.
The global symlink will be removed.
The consuming project will not have the symlink and cannot use the library.
questions.explanation: Without both steps, the symlink does not exist in your consuming project.

questions.question: How does npm link enable immediate reflection of library changes in the consuming project?
options: By publishing the library to a private npm registry.
By creating a global symlink and then a local symlink in the consuming project.
By installing the latest version from npm automatically.
By copying the library files into the consuming project.
questions.explanation: npm link creates a global symlink and then a local symlink in the consuming project, so changes in the library source are immediately reflected.

questions.question: Why is it necessary to run npm link inside the library directory before linking it in the consuming project?
options: Because it publishes the package to a private registry
Because it compiles the library source code
Because it registers the package globally by creating a global symlink
Because it installs the package from the npm registry
questions.explanation: Running npm link inside the library directory registers the package globally by creating a global symlink from the package into the global node_modules.

questions.question: What is a potential issue if the global symlink created by npm link is missing or incorrectly set up?
options: The consuming project will not have a local symlink pointing to the library, so changes won't be reflected
The consuming project will automatically download the latest version from npm
The library will be published to npm unintentionally
The TypeScript compiler will fail to run in watch mode
questions.explanation: If the global symlink does not exist, the consuming project cannot create a local symlink pointing to the library, so changes in the library won't be reflected in the consuming project.

questions.question: What are the two steps involved in using npm link correctly?
options: Run npm link <package-name> in the consuming project, then npm link in the library.
Run npm install in the library, then npm publish.
Run npm uninstall in the consuming project, then npm link in the library.
Run npm link inside the library, then npm link <package-name> in the consuming project.
questions.explanation: npm link is a two-step process: npm link in the library, then npm link <package-name> in the consuming project.

questions.question: Why is npm link considered essential for local library development workflows?
options: Because it allows testing without publishing and speeds up development.
Because it deletes old versions of your library.
Because it installs dependencies faster than npm install.
Because it automatically publishes your library to npm.
questions.explanation: npm link is essential because it lets you develop and test your library without publishing, saving time and avoiding version bumps.

questions.question: If you want to test a local library in a consuming project, what is the correct order of commands?
options: Run npm install inside the library, then npm publish.
Run npm link <package-name> in the consuming project, then npm link inside the library.
Run npm uninstall in the consuming project, then npm link inside the library.
Run npm link inside the library, then npm link <package-name> in the consuming project.
